title: Partnership, communication and person-centred relationships
blurb: Work in partnership with women, involve partners and family on her terms, and use independent interpreters well.
question: At booking, a woman who speaks little English attends with her husband, who offers to interpret. The midwife needs to ask about mental health, previous pregnancies and domestic abuse. What is the most appropriate action?

teach.body: SPM 1.13 asks midwives to work in partnership with women, basing care on each woman's needs, views, preferences and decisions, and strengthening her own capabilities to care for herself and her baby. Partnership means sharing power: the midwife brings evidence and skill, the woman brings knowledge of her own life and values, and decisions are made together. In plain English: it is her pregnancy, and the midwife is her expert companion.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives (2019) 1.10 to 1.13; Code 2.1 to 2.4

teach.h: Partners and family: on her terms
teach.body: SPM 1.10 asks midwives to involve partners and family in discussions and decisions about her care and the baby's care, always respecting the woman's preferences about who to involve and to what extent. She decides. That is why every woman should have an opportunity for a private, one-to-one discussion without her partner present (NG201 1.2.5): it is the time to ask safely about domestic abuse and other sensitive issues. For women with complex social factors, CG110 1.1.14 asks for a one-to-one consultation on at least one occasion.

teach.caption: Use professional interpreting services (spoken languages, British Sign Language, Makaton) that are independent of the woman.

steps.label: Teach-back
steps.sub: She explains it in her words

teach.caption: NICE NG197 shared decision making 1.2.11 and 1.2.17; NG235 1.4.8 asks you to confirm she has understood.

head: SPM
Proficiency
rows: Involve partner and family as she chooses

teach.body: Parwana speaks Dari and attends booking with her husband, who offers to interpret. Midwife Sian thanks him but books a professional Dari interpreter by phone. She explains that part of every appointment is spent with the woman alone, and asks him to wait outside for that part. With the interpreter, she asks about Parwana's mental health, previous births and routine enquiry about domestic abuse, checks understanding, and records Parwana's language need so an interpreter is booked for every contact.

items.label: standard of care whatever she decides

teach.caption: Tone and demeanour matter as much as the actual words used (NG235 1.4.10). Treat every woman with kindness, dignity and respect (1.4.9).

teach.text: A family member who speaks English well is still not an appropriate interpreter for clinical consultations, even if the woman seems happy with it. And a woman's partner is involved to the extent SHE chooses: partnership is with the woman, not with the couple by default.

items: Partnership (SPM 1.13): care built on her needs, views, preferences and decisions, strengthening her own capabilities.
Partners and family are involved as and when she chooses (SPM 1.10); make sure she has a private one-to-one opportunity (NG201 1.2.5; CG110 1.1.14).
Use independent professional interpreters, not partners, family or friends (NG235 1.4.8; CG110 1.3.10).
Plain language, chunk and check, teach-back; record what mattered to her (NG197).
She can accept or decline care and change her mind, and her decisions do not change how she is cared for (NG235 1.4.10).

summary: You can now describe partnership working with women, involve partners and family in the way the woman chooses, and choose an independent interpreter. You can use plain language, chunk and check and teach-back to make sure information is understood.

A.q: A woman who speaks Polish attends an antenatal appointment with her 16-year-old daughter, who speaks fluent English. What is the most appropriate way to communicate?
options: Ask the daughter to interpret
Use a professional Polish interpreter
Use a translation app on a phone
Speak slowly using simple English
A.why: NG235 1.4.8 and CG110 1.3.10: use reliable interpreting services that are independent of the woman, rather than a family member or friend.

whyNot.0: Family members, especially children, are not independent and may not interpret accurately or confidentially.
whyNot.2: A phone app is not a reliable interpreting service for clinical conversations.
whyNot.3: Simplified English does not meet her language need.

A.q: A woman says she would like her mother, but not her partner, to be present when her test results are discussed. What should the midwife do?
options: Invite both so the family hears the same thing
Arrange the discussion as she has asked
Explain that partners are usually present
Ask the partner whether he agrees
A.why: SPM 1.10: involve partner and family always respecting the woman's preferences and decisions about who to involve and to what extent.

whyNot.0: Inviting the partner overrides her choice.
whyNot.2: There is no expectation that partners attend; she decides.
whyNot.3: The partner's agreement is not needed; it is her information and her decision.

A.q: Which technique best checks that a woman has understood information about a screening test?
options: Asking whether she has any questions
Giving her a printed leaflet to read
Repeating the information more slowly
Asking her to explain it in her own words
A.why: Teach-back (asking her to explain in her own words) checks understanding; NG197 1.2.11 recommends chunk and check and teach-back.

whyNot.0: Many people say they have no questions without having understood.
whyNot.1: A leaflet supports discussion but does not check understanding.
whyNot.2: Repetition does not show whether she has understood.

B.q: At every antenatal contact so far, a woman's partner has answered questions for her. When is the best opportunity to ask her about domestic abuse?
options: During the next contact, with her partner present
At a contact where she is seen on her own
By telephone at a time her partner chooses
At her 6-week postnatal check with the GP
B.why: NG201 1.2.5: ask about domestic abuse at booking or at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, with a private one-to-one discussion; CG110 1.1.14 says offer at least one consultation without her partner.

whyNot.0: Asking in front of a possible abuser is unsafe and unlikely to lead to disclosure.
whyNot.2: A call arranged around her partner may not be private.
whyNot.3: Delaying until after the birth misses the chance to protect her and the baby during pregnancy.

B.q: A Deaf woman who uses British Sign Language is admitted in labour. Her hearing sister offers to sign. What is the best plan?
options: Accept her sister's offer for now
Rely on written notes during labour
Use lip-reading with clear speech
Book a registered BSL interpreter
B.why: NG235 1.4.8 names British Sign Language among languages needing reliable, independent interpreting services. Her sister can support her as a birth companion.

whyNot.0: A relative is not independent, and may not interpret clinical information accurately.
whyNot.1: Written notes are slow and impractical in labour and may not match her first language.
whyNot.2: Lip-reading is unreliable, especially in labour, and is not her preferred language.

B.q: A midwife wants to build a trusting relationship with a woman who had a traumatic first birth. Which approach best reflects SPM 1.12 and 1.13?
options: Ask her what matters most to her this time
Reassure her this birth will be different
Advise a planned caesarean to avoid repeats
Suggest she avoids reading her old notes
B.why: Partnership starts with her needs, views and preferences (SPM 1.13) and builds a trusting, respectful relationship (1.12).

whyNot.1: False reassurance can damage trust; nobody can promise a birth outcome.
whyNot.2: Mode of birth should be discussed in partnership, not directed by the midwife.
whyNot.3: She has the right to read her records, and doing so may help her.

C.q: During a birth planning discussion with an interpreter present, a woman's mother-in-law interrupts repeatedly and answers for her. What should the midwife do first?
options: Ask the interpreter to translate the mother-in-law's answers
Ask the woman who she wants present for the discussion
Postpone the discussion until the next appointment
Direct her questions to the mother-in-law instead
C.why: SPM 1.10: the woman decides who is involved and to what extent. Asking her (through the interpreter) restores her voice; the midwife may then need to see her alone.

whyNot.0: This hears the mother-in-law's views, not the woman's.
whyNot.2: Postponing delays her care and does not address the problem.
whyNot.3: Directing questions away from the woman undermines partnership.

C.q: A woman in labour declines continuous fetal monitoring. Later she says she worries the team is annoyed with her. What should the midwife say?
options: The team will record that she declined
She can change her mind if she wishes
The team will keep giving her the same care
The team prefers women to follow advice
C.why: NG235 1.4.10: support the woman so she understands she can accept or decline care, can change her mind, and that her decisions will not affect how care is provided. Her worry is about how she will be treated.

whyNot.0: Documentation is needed, but it does not address her worry about being treated differently.
whyNot.1: This is true but, said now, can sound like pressure to accept rather than reassurance.
whyNot.3: This suggests disapproval and undermines her right to decline.

C.q: A midwife explains gestational diabetes testing to a woman with a learning disability, who nods throughout. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Record that consent has been given
Repeat the information to her partner
Check understanding using teach-back
Give a leaflet and book the test
C.why: Nodding is not evidence of understanding. Teach-back, with adapted or easy-read information (for example a healthcare passport), checks understanding before she decides.

whyNot.0: Consent needs her to understand; nodding does not show that.
whyNot.1: Telling her partner does not check her own understanding.
whyNot.3: A standard leaflet may not meet her needs, and the test is booked before she has understood.

reteach.title: Whose voice comes first?
reteach.question: In a room with a woman, her partner, her mother and an interpreter, whose voice comes first, and how do you make sure it is heard?

blocks.body: The woman's voice comes first. Ask her who she wants involved. Use an independent interpreter so her words reach you unfiltered. See her alone at least once so she can tell you things she cannot say in front of others. Explain things in plain language and check she has understood with teach-back.

blocks.text: A fluent family member is not an interpreter. Independent means not connected to the woman, so she can speak freely and be understood accurately.

explain.body: SPM 1.13: base care on her needs, views, preferences and decisions, and strengthen her own capabilities. Code 2.3: encourage and empower people to share decisions.

test.q: Which statement best describes partnership working in midwifery?
options: The midwife decides and explains the reasons
The woman decides with no professional input
Decisions are shared, based on her preferences
The family agrees a plan with the midwife
test.why: Partnership means sharing decisions, combining evidence with the woman's needs, views and preferences (SPM 1.13).

whyNot.1: Partnership includes the midwife's evidence and advice.
whyNot.3: The partnership is with the woman; family are involved as she chooses.

explain.body: SPM 1.10: involve partner and family on her terms. CG110 1.1.14: at least one consultation without her partner. NG201 1.2.5: ask about domestic abuse when she is alone, in a private one-to-one discussion.

steps.label: Explain
steps.sub: Part of every booking is one-to-one

test.q: Why should a woman be offered at least one antenatal consultation without her partner?
options: To complete the booking forms more quickly
To reduce infection risk from extra visitors
To check his consent to the plan of care
To allow safe disclosure of sensitive issues
test.why: Seeing her alone allows routine enquiry about domestic abuse and disclosure of sensitive issues safely (CG110 1.1.14; NG201 1.2.5).

whyNot.1: Infection control is not the purpose of a one-to-one consultation.
whyNot.2: Her partner's consent is not needed for her care.

explain.body: NG235 1.4.8: reliable interpreting services, independent of the woman, rather than a family member or friend; includes BSL and Makaton. CG110 1.3.10 says the same for women with complex social factors.

test.q: A woman's partner is a qualified interpreter in her language. Should he interpret at her booking appointment?
options: Yes, because he holds a qualification
Yes, if she says she is happy with it
No, because he is not independent of her
No, unless the trust interpreter is busy
test.why: The key test is independence: interpreters should be independent of the woman. A partner is not, whatever his qualifications.

whyNot.0: A qualification does not make him independent of her.
whyNot.1: She may feel unable to refuse in front of him; independence protects safe disclosure.
whyNot.3: A busy service is a reason to book or use telephone interpreting, not to use her partner.

explain.body: Code 7.1 plain terms; 7.4 check understanding. NG197: chunk and check, teach-back, record what mattered. NG235 1.4.10: tone and demeanour matter as much as words.

steps.label:
Ask her to
say it back

test.q: Which Code standard asks registrants to check people's understanding from time to time?
test.why: Code 7.4: check people's understanding from time to time to keep misunderstanding or mistakes to a minimum.

whyNot.1: 5.2 is about telling people how their information is used and shared.
whyNot.2: 9.1 is about giving honest feedback to colleagues.
whyNot.3: 10.4 is about attributing, dating and timing record entries.
